4. The Minister then posed a question who are protecting criminals and terrorists?" He referred to an accused in a murder case named Nurunnabi, who was granted advance bail by the Court. He felt sorry when he saw that one Nurunnabi involved in the bomb attack that killed several people at Udichi Conference in Jessore, got advance bail from the Court. 

 11. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Attorney-General, appeared before the Court and submitted that he is not appearing on behalf of the illegal contemner, rather he is appearing as Attorney-General on behalf of the Government in view of the fact that a notice of this application was given to him and he found that questions of interpretation of several provisions of the Constitution are involved in this case and, as such, he felt that he should appear to assist the Court in this matter. 

 16. Mr Moudud Ahmed further submits that the statements made by the Home Minister in the Parliament are very much wide and general in nature and it has, in fact, affected the independence of judiciary and the judicial functions of the Judges of the Superior Courts. He further submits that though two instances have been given by the Home Minister in Parliament, one with regard to granting of bail to a terrorist named Shubhra of Maghbazar and another Mr Nurunnabi, an accused in a bomb case, yet those instances are not correct inasmuch as that Nurunnabi of Jessore is still in custody and the Shubhra of Maghbazar was not granted bail by the High Court Division in any case. He has produced before us a copy of the judgment of Writ Petition No. 1607 of 1999 which was heard and disposed of on 11-7-1999 by a Division Bench of this Court. In that writ petition the detention of the said Shubhra was challenged. From the judgment it appears that Shubhra was first detained under the Special Powers Act and the order of detention was challenged in the High Court Division in a writ petition. After hearing the High Court Division made the Rule absolute, declared the detention illegal and directed the respondents to release him. Thrice detention orders were passed and on three occasions the High Court Division declared the detention of Shubhra illegal and directed the respondents to release the detenu. But it appears from the judgment that as soon as the detenu came out from jail gate, every time he was served with the fresh detention order and kept him in custody on the selfsame grounds and reasons. 

 17. Similarly, for the fourth time a similar detention order was served upon Shubhra at the jail gate and under that order he was kept in custody and this fourth detention order was challenged in Writ Petition No. 1607 of 1999. In that case Mr Abdul Baset Majumder, the learned Advocate appeared for the petitioner and Mr Md Layakuzzaman, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appeared for the Government. In delivering the judgment the Division Bench made a detailed discussion about the arrest of the detenu Shubhra for the fourth time one after another on the same and similar grounds. 

 In disposing of the detention case the High Court Division held that only for frustrating the judgment of the High Court Division the successive orders of the detention were given which is nothing but interference with the course of justice. Further, the High Court Division directed the detaining authority not to repeat such an illegal detention order in order to frustrate the judgment of the High Court Division. Further, a copy of the judgment was sent to the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs for information and for taking necessary actions for such repeated illegal detention orders on the selfsame grounds to a citizen of this country. So, Mr Moudud Ahmed submits that the statement of the Home Minister was not at all correct inasmuch as Shubhra was not granted bail by the High Court Division, rather his detentions were declared illegal four times one after another and the Court desired that such repetition of illegal arrest and detention should not be made in future on identical grounds. So, Mr Moudud Ahmed submits that on the basis of wrong information and misrepresentation the Home Minister made a statement Shubhra about of Maghbazar in the Parliament which is not at all correct. As regards the statement on Nurunnabi it is submitted by Mr Moudud Ahmed that he is still in custody. 

 18. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Attorney-General, appeared on behalf of the Government in this case. Mr Attorney-General submits that during question and answer hour the Home Minister made statements in the Parliament on question put by a lady, Member of Parliament and this question and answer in the Parliament is very much a part of the proceeding of Parliament as per Rule 41 of the Rules of Procedure which speaks that unless the Speaker otherwise directs, the first hour of every sitting shall be available for the asking and answering of questions. Mr Attorney-General submits that the Rules of Procedure of Parliament of the People's Republic of Bangladesh was enacted under Article 5(1)(a) of the Constitution. Since these Rules of Procedure of Parliament have been enacted under the authority of the Constitution it is very much a law. Mr Attorney-General has drawn our attention to Article 108 of the Constitution. He submits that the power of the High Court Division in order to investigate into and punish any contempt of this Court is subject to law. He submits that Rules of Procedure of Parliament is a law and Article 78(3) of the Constitution is a substantive provision of the Constitution. So, he submits that in pursuance of the provision of Article 78(3) of the Constitution read with Rule 270 of the Rules of Procedure of Parliament the Members of Parliament are immune from any proceeding in a Court if the Member of Parliament makes statement in Parliament and in course of the business of the Parliament. He submits that Article 108 is not absolute rather it is subject to law. 

 20. In support of his contention Mr Attorney-General has referred to the case of Cyril Sikdar vs Nazmul Huda, 46 DLR 555. We have gone through this judgment delivered by a Division Bench of this Court and it appears to us that the facts and points of law of that case are more or less identical with those of the present case. In that case Mr Nazmul Huda, a Member of Parliament and the then Information Minister made a statement in the Parliament about Mr Akhtaruzzaman Chowdhury Babu, the then MP of Awami League relating to his involvement in a murder case which was sub judice in the Court of law. At that time the present Prime Minister who was then the Leader of the Opposition spoke in the Parliament stating that objectionable statements of the Information Minister were very much contemptuous. 

 21. On such matter Mr Cyril Sikdar a practicing Advocate of this Court, filed a case before this Court being Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 835 of 1993 (Contempt). This matter was heard at length by a Division Bench of this Court. In that case Mr KS Nabi with Mr Subrata Chowdhury appeared for the petitioner and Mr Abdul Wadud Khandaker, Additional Attorney-General with Mr Syed Abu Kowsar, Assistant Attorney-General appeared for the State. It clearly appears from the aforesaid judgment that the Information Minister in course of discussion in the Parliament made certain statements and remarks about a pending case with regard to involvement of Mr Akhtaruzzarnan Chowdhury Babu, an Opposition MP and that was the subject matter for decision in the aforesaid Criminal Miscellaneous Case. A Division Bench of this Court comprising Mr Justice Fazle Hussain Mohammad Habibur Rahman and Mr Justice Mainur Reza Chowdhury passed the judgment rejecting the contempt application summarily. 

 22. Mr Attorney-General is relying upon the aforesaid judgment of this Court inasmuch as the facts and circumstances and also points of law involved in the instant case are more or less identical with those of the aforesaid reported case. In disposing of the aforesaid case the Division Bench took much pains and considered several decisions of the Indian Jurisdiction and several provisions of the Constitution of the India as well as the; provisions of Bill of Rights, 1689 and also the Constitution of the United States of America. In that case specifically, like the present one, Article 78(3) of our Constitution was the subject matter for consideration. Their Lordships considered Article 105(2) of the Constitution of India, the Bill of Rights of 1689 the Constitution of the United States of America and the reported cases of Indian jurisdiction namely, the cases reported in AIR 1965 (SC) 745 and Tei Kiran and others vs M Sanjiva Reddy and others, AIR 1970(SC) 1573 and specifically Article 121 and Article 221 of the Constitution of India. It appears that it is a learned judgment of their Lordships and we should not repeat the quotations made by their Lordships in that judgment since we are referring the judgment itself in the instant case. 

 23. It is held in the case reported in AIR 1965 (SC) 745 by their Lordships that "the Constitution makers attached so much importance to the necessity of absolute freedom in debates within the legislative chambers that they thought it necessary to confer complete immunity on the legislators from any action in any court in respect of their speeches in the legislative chambers in the wide terms prescribed by clause (2) of Article 105. Thus, clause (1) confers freedom of speech on the legislators within the legislative chamber and clause (2) makes it plain that the freedom is literally absolute and unfettered". 

 26. Considering the above we are of the view that the view taken by the Division Bench of this Court in the case of Cyril Sikdar vs Nazmul Huda is very much applicable in the instant case and there is no reason to take a different view by us from the view taken by their Lordships in the aforesaid case. 

 His Lordship observed," the internal and proper business of the proceeding of the Parliament is beyond the purview of the Constitutional Court, but while acting in the name of internal proceeding, if any violation of Constitutional provision takes place then this Court is certainly competent to interfere". Relying upon the above observation Mr Moudud Ahmed submits that though the immunity is given to a Member of Parliament in Article 78(3) of the Constitution it is not absolute and it is subject to the Article 78(3) of the Constitution did not come directly for consideration of their Lordships of the Appellate Division and from the observation made by his Lordship Latifur Rahman J it appears that if any Constitutional provision is violated then the learned Advocate for the petitioner has failed to action may be taken. But in the instant case the show that any Constitutional provision has been violated by the Home Minister in making statement in the Parliament. In this view of the matter we find that the above judgment is not of any assistance to Mr Moudud Ahmed. 

 "The Minister then posed a question, who are protecting criminals and terrorists? Mr Nasim also referred to an accused in a murder case, Nurunnabi who was granted ad-interim bail by the High Court". 

 33. Prima facie it appears that such statements are very much objectionable, highly contemptuous and glaring examples of interference with administration of justice and judicial functions of the Judges of the highest Court. Had these statements been made outside the Parliament the situation would have been otherwise and it would have been considered in a different way. But in the instant case the statements have been made by a Member of Parliament in the Parliament and during the business transaction of the Parliament. This is' the crux of the whole problem in the instant case. The statements have been made by a Member of Parliament who is the Home Minister of the Government. We cannot but mention that Mr Nasim has been holding a responsible and Constitutional Post as a Minister of the Government. Further, we can take judicial notice of one fact that Mr Nasim is not only a Member of Parliament and the Home Minister, but also a son of a renowned Lawyer and a valiant freedom fighter late Captain Mansur Ali who was once the Prime Minister of this country, So, it is expected that in making the above statements in the Parliament Mr Nasim should have taken more care and caution as his statements related to the judicial functions of the Constitutional Judges of the Supreme Court. 

 36. The statements as appearing in the newspapers as annexed with the application prima facie show that they are objectionable and contemptuous, but in the instant case that cannot be a ground for prosecution of a Member of Parliament under the law of Contempt of Court for the reasons discussed above. We have given our anxious consideration over the matter and we are of the view that there is no merit in this application as the immunity under Article 78(3) of the Constitution is absolute and unqualified. But before parting with the case we may observe in the language of our Appellate Division that the Court expected more circumspection, understanding, discretion and judgment on the part of a Member of Parliament who is the Home Minister of the Government because of the high office he holds in making the statements in Parliament regarding the judicial functions of the Constitutional Judges of the highest Court of the country. 

 37. Following the decision of the Division Bench of this Court as. referred to above and the consistent views of the Indian Supreme Court with regard to immunity of the Members of Parliament within the Parliament, we are of the view, this is not a fit case where we should interfere and issue a contempt Rule. For the reasons as discussed above and with the observations as we have made, this application for drawing up a Contempt of Court proceeding against the Home Minister Mr Nasim is summarily rejected.
